summary_paraphrase: A small boy is startled four times (by something in a bush, a crash at bedtime, a box by the door, a dark empty house) and each time cries out for Mmawe; each time a voice tells him not to be scared and names the harmless cause: a new dog, a falling pot, new shoes, and finally his father coming home.

characters.name: Tshedza
characters.change: none stated; his last line turns from fear to missing someone

characters.name: Mmawe
characters.relation_to_protagonist: the adult he calls; INFERRED his mother (shown mostly from the waist down)

characters.name: Baba
characters.relation_to_protagonist: father; the last scare and the last comfort

characters.name: Banda
characters.relation_to_protagonist: Makhulu's new dog; first scare, then playmate

characters.name: Makhulu
characters.relation_to_protagonist: grandmother, named only as Banda's owner

humor_notes: The scream is drawn in the same arms-up pose every time, so the fourth repeat is funny as well as tense; the causes are comically ordinary.

repetition.description: The title cry, the boy screaming for Mmawe, on four spreads
repetition.why: a listener can shout it with him; the pose and lettering never change, only the background, which darkens at the end

repetition.description: The answer line 'don't be scared, Tshedza, it's just ...' on four spreads, each with a new ordinary cause
repetition.why: the predictable comfort line lets the child expect safety; only the cause changes, so the child guesses it

repetition.description: Unknown, scream, harmless answer: four rounds
repetition.why: short rounds that always land safely

notes: The picture lets the listener see the answer before the boy does: a tail in the bush on page 1, a snake-like red lace curling out of the box on page 7.
The comforting adult is cropped to the waist on pages 3 and 9, keeping the camera at the child's height; her face appears only in the bedtime kiss.
The fourth scream reuses the same drawing with every colour dimmed: escalation carried by palette alone.
White space and hand lettering give each scream a full page of its own, a quiet frame for a loud line.

strengths: a refrain a pre-reader can shout
a second refrain that always delivers comfort
the picture lets the child solve the scare first
ordinary causes make fear safe to play with
weaknesses: the child never resolves a fear himself; an adult always explains
no growth: he screams the same way at the end

anti_patterns.note: every scare is defused by an adult's explanation; fitting for 3-4 but the child has no agency
Tshedza's only action in a scare is to call for help

child_appeal_heuristic.label: Research heuristic — not validated
child_appeal_heuristic.rationale: Scores are the analyst's reading of the pages, not observations of children.

age_suitability.notes: Mild, comic scares that always resolve as harmless; the dark-house spread is the strongest and is answered on the very next page. The scream refrain is loud; not a bedtime read.

metrics.lexicon_note: direct_address and sound_words are lexicon counts: a floor, not a measure. direct_address counts second-person words anywhere, dialogue included — it is not narrator-to-reader address

repetition.end_rhyme_note: heuristic: consecutive lines sharing a final two letters

a crash, a box, a dark house

craft.writer_note: A fear pattern that repeats four times needs its last round to change the answer (here, the scare is the person he missed). An adult explains every scare; a child explaining one would raise agency.
